turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through, both of you. How are you going with all this?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, good. Parking was a shocker out the front, took us ten minutes to find a spot. This'll be quick, yeah?
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It won't be quick. I've been a mess since that letter.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me what's been on your mind. What made you book in?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Uh, the camp reckons I've got thalassaemia trait. She's pregnant, so they want her to have bloods. That's why we're here, nothing dramatic.
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm sixteen weeks... sorry, fifteen weeks and a bit, sixteen on Thursday. And I keep thinking about the baby.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): She's spiralling. I'm not. They said trait, not the disease. Big difference.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): What do you remember them saying on the day?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, it was six weeks back... no, three weeks. Community camp at the town hall, finger prick, then a letter. Carrier, see your GP if your partner's pregnant. That's all.
[SEG0010] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Three weeks of me googling at midnight. He pretends it's fine.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah nah. I can't hear myself think in our flat with those podcasts going half the night. Doesn't make me a patient.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. And in yourself, day to day, how have you been feeling?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm alright. I feel like a wet rag when I get home, but I've overdone it. Long shifts, that's all.
[SEG0014] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's not alright. His feet have been going numb for a couple of months and he just waves it off.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): They have not. My feet feel dead at the end of a shift, last few days, not months. It's nothing.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. So between you I'm hearing a few days up to a couple of months, and you don't quite land in the same place. I'll note it as roughly that span.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): And there's a frog in my throat some mornings. Aircon at the warehouse. Hardly a thing.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Aside from the feet and the throat, any chest pain, or getting puffed when you walk?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): What tablets are you taking these days? Just so I've got the list.

[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodopine for the pressure, in the morning. I was on five milligrams... no, they bumped me, it's ten. The cholesterol one at night, atorvastaton, eighty... no, forty milligrams. Sugar tablets, metforman, five hundred twice a day, and only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning, a teaspoon stirred in water.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thanks. I wouldn't stop any of those off the back of a camp letter.
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Even that shop powder? I keep saying it's not real medicine.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): It's just powder. Leave it. My auntie uses the same stuff.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anyone in your family with thalassaemia, or anaemia that needed transfusions?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nobody. Mum's side are all fine.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the worry side, how has that been sitting with you?
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's anxious. He checks that letter every night, he just won't admit it.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not anxious. She's the anxious one. I glance at it, that's all.

[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright. My working impression is this is the trait, the carrier state, not thalassaemia disease. That fits the camp letter and what you've told me. It only really matters for the bub if your wife carries it as well.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): See? Storm in a teacup. We could've sorted this over the phone.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): I still want her tested properly. I'll order a full blood count and a haemoglobin electrophoresis, the proper screen, not another finger prick.
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Can we do it tomorrow? I don't want to sit on this.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yep, no worries. I'll send the request now and reception can book you tomorrow morning.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): And if hers comes back normal we just drop it, right?

[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): If hers is normal, this doesn't put the bub at risk of the severe illness. If she comes back as a carrier too, I'll refer you both for genetic counselling so you can talk the options through with someone who does this every day.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Counselling. More talking. Brilliant.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's worth doing if we land there. Either way I'll see you both back here in two weeks, once the results are in.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We'll come. Thank you, really.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Fine. Still reckon it's a fuss.

[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep on the morning blood pressure tablet, the night one, the sugar tablets and that powder, just as you are. If the feet get worse, or you get chest pain, don't wait for me, get seen sooner.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, yeah. Of. See you in a fortnight.

spec.situation: Couple, wife pregnant, husband found to carry thalassaemia trait at a camp; both anxious; blood tests for the wife planned; genetic counselling discussed.

traps.happens: The patient lists medicines with their purpose ('amlodipine for the pressure', 'the cholesterol one at night', 'sugar tablets') and also mentions a herbal or shop remedy in passing ('only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning'). Their chronic conditions are never asked about directly.
traps.label_rule: Each medicine is recorded with the dose and timing said for THAT medicine; the herbal remedy is a medicine too (currently_used). A condition the patient states through its medicine ('for the pressure') is a past_medical_history entry ONLY if the patient actually said the condition name or its everyday name ('the pressure' = hypertension, normalized); do not invent a duration.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

features: self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
